# **Rotation Robustness in Galaxy Morphology Classification**

**Course:** Deep Learning, Tel Aviv University, 2026

**Lecturer:** Shay Palachy Affek

**Students:** Ariel Sobol and Guy Berelzon 

**Dataset:** Galaxy10 DECaLS

## **1\. Introduction**

### **1.1 Background**

Modern sky surveys photograph hundreds of millions of galaxies. The shape of a galaxy, called its morphology, tells astronomers how it formed and how it has evolved. Sorting galaxies by shape is therefore useful, but doing it by hand at this scale is impossible.

The Galaxy Zoo project handled this by recruiting volunteers to classify images, which shows how much manual effort the task normally takes.

### **1.2 The problem**

We wanted to know whether a neural network can do this job automatically, and more specifically, whether it does the job in a way that makes physical sense.

Here is the point that makes the problem interesting. A galaxy has no correct orientation. A spiral photographed at 0 degrees and the same spiral photographed at 90 degrees are the same object, and the label should not change. A model that has really learned morphology should therefore give the same answer no matter how the image is turned. A standard CNN has no built-in guarantee of this. Pooling gives it some tolerance to shifts, but nothing in its design makes it invariant to rotation.

So the question is not only “can the model classify galaxies”, but **“does it classify them for the right reasons”.**

### **1.3 Task definition**

**Input:** one 256x256 colour image of a single galaxy.

**Output:** a probability for each of 10 morphology classes. The highest one is the prediction.

**Task type:** single-image, multi-class classification.

A CNN suits this task because the distinguishing features (smooth blobs, spiral arms, thin edge-on streaks) are subtle and vary from galaxy to galaxy.

### **1.4 Research question**

**To what extent is a transfer-learning CNN invariant to rotations and flips in galaxy morphology classification, and to what degree do data augmentation versus architectural choices improve its robustness?**

We split this into three sub-questions:

1. How much does the baseline’s accuracy drop when test images are rotated and flipped, and why?  
2. Does training with rotation and flip augmentation restore that accuracy?  
3. Do architectural choices affect robustness to rotation?

## **2\. The dataset**

### **2.1 What we needed**

To answer the research question we needed three things: images paired with shape labels, enough data to train a deep network, and a clean download that did not require assembling the dataset ourselves.

### **2.2 Galaxy10 DECaLS**

Galaxy10 DECaLS met all three requirements.

| Property | Value |
| :---- | :---- |
| Number of images | 17,736 |
| Image size | 256 x 256, color (3 channels) |
| Classes | 10 morphology types |
| Label source | Galaxy Zoo volunteer votes |
| Image source | DECaLS survey |
| Format | HDF5 (.h5) |

The file contains six arrays: images, ans (the labels), plus ra, dec, redshift and pxscale. We used the first two.

The ten classes are:

| ID | Class | ID | Class |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 0 | Disturbed | 5 | Barred Spiral |
| 1 | Merging | 6 | Unbarred Tight Spiral |
| 2 | Round Smooth | 7 | Unbarred Loose Spiral |
| 3 | In-between Round Smooth | 8 | Edge-on without Bulge |
| 4 | Cigar-shaped Smooth | 9 | Edge-on with Bulge |

### **2.3 Datasets we considered and rejected**

| Dataset | Why we did not use it |
| :---- | :---- |
| NED-LVS | A catalogue of about 2 million objects, but it holds tabular physical properties such as distance and redshift. It contains no images and no shape labels. |
| GalaxiesML | 286,000 images, but no discrete shape classes. It provides continuous structural parameters and redshifts, and uses 5-band data which complicates standard 3-channel transfer learning. It is built for redshift regression. |
| Galaxy Zoo 2 | Rich hierarchical labels for 304,000 galaxies, but the images have to be downloaded and matched to the label catalogue by hand. |
| Galaxy10 SDSS | A workable lighter fallback with 21,785 images, but at only 69x69 pixels the image quality is much lower. |

## **3\. EDA**

### **3.1 First look at the raw data**

Before anything we looked at what an image actually is. Each image is a 256x256x3 array of integers from 0 to 255, which is 196,608 numbers per galaxy. We printed a small corner of one image to see the raw values, then located the brightest pixel and compared a bright patch near the galaxy centre against a dark patch of background sky. The bright patch reached values above 250 while the background patch sat mostly below 60\. This confirmed the basic structure of these images: a small bright object on a large dark background.

### **3.2 Class distribution**

The classes are not balanced:

| Class | Images | Share |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Round Smooth | 2,645 | 14.9% |
| Unbarred Loose Spiral | 2,628 | 14.8% |
| Barred Spiral | 2,043 | 11.5% |
| In-between Smooth | 2,027 | 11.4% |
| Edge-on with Bulge | 1,873 | 10.6% |
| Merging | 1,853 | 10.4% |
| Unbarred Tight Spiral | 1,829 | 10.3% |
| Edge-on without Bulge | 1,423 | 8.0% |
| Disturbed | 1,081 | 6.1% |
| Cigar-shaped Smooth | 334 | 1.9% |

The gap between the largest and smallest class is about 8 to 1\. This matters because overall accuracy can look acceptable while the model performs badly on the rare classes. For this reason we report per-class precision and recall along with a confusion matrix throughout the project, not just a single accuracy number.

![][image1]

### **3.3 Visual examples**

We looked at one example from each class, and then at several examples from a single class to see how much variation exists inside one category.

Some classes are visually obvious. The edge-on galaxies are thin streaks and the round smooth ones are clean blobs but thers are much harder. The three spiral types differ only in how tightly the arms wind and whether a central bar is present, which is a matter of degree rather than a clear visual break. 

**![][image2]**

### **3.4 Data quality check**

We checked whether any images were blank or corrupted. We measured the pixel standard deviation of every image, computed in batches to avoid loading all the data into memory at once. A blank or broken image would have very little variation, so we flagged the lowest 1 percent as suspicious. This flagged 178 images.

**The problem with that test:** There is always a lowest 1 percent, so flagging alone proves nothing. The real test is the shape of the distribution. If genuinely broken images existed, the histogram would show a small cluster separated from the rest. What we saw was a smooth hill with no separate group.

**Where the flagged images came from:** We then checked which classes the flagged images belonged to. Round Smooth accounted for 78 of the 178, far more than any other class. That makes sense, because a smooth featureless galaxy genuinely has low pixel variation. The flagged images were not broken data, they were simply the flattest-looking galaxies.

**Conclusion:** No corrupted or blank images in the dataset.

**![][image3]**

### **3.5 Framing and centering check**

Since we planned to rotate these images, we needed to know how much of the frame each galaxy fills. A galaxy that reaches the edge of the frame could get clipped when the image is rotated.

**First attempt, which failed:** We used a simple brightness threshold to measure the fraction of the frame occupied by the galaxy. It returned a median of 0.99, meaning nearly every galaxy filled its entire frame  and that is clearly wrong. The problem was background stars: bright pixels scattered across the frame were being counted as part of the galaxy.

**The fix:** We changed the measurement to look only at the largest connected bright region, which is the galaxy itself, and ignore isolated bright pixels elsewhere. This gave a median occupancy of 0.33, which is realistic.

**Result:** With the corrected measurement, 49 out of 300 sampled images had occupancy above 0.7, meaning they sit close enough to the frame edge that rotation could clip them. Broken down by class, the highest rates were Edge-on without Bulge at 32% percent and Merging at 22.9%. This gave us a specific prediction to test later: if clipping matters, these two classes should suffer most under rotation.

### **![][image4]3.6 Chirality check**

Spiral galaxies have a handedness: their arms wind either clockwise or counter-clockwise. Flipping an image reverses that handedness and we wanted to know whether this changes what the galaxy is.

We displayed spiral galaxies alongside their horizontally and vertically flipped versions, and did the same for Round Smooth galaxies as a contrast case. A flipped spiral is still a spiral of the same type, so flipping is a label-preserving operation here. This justified including flips in the augmentation later.

### **3.7 Color statistics**

Color does not change when an image is rotated. If color alone could separate the classes, that part of the task would be immune to rotation, and our whole research question would matter less.

We computed per-channel means and standard deviations across the dataset in batches, then per-class channel means. The images use the DECaLS grz convention, where the g band (shortest wavelength) is stored in blue, r in green, and z (longest) in red.

The overall per-channel means are 37.2, 36.0 and 35.6 on a 0 to 255 scale, with standard deviations of 33.9, 31.1 and 29.3. The means being around 14% of the maximum confirms that these images are mostly dark sky with a small bright galaxy, which is very different from typical everyday photographs.

Across classes, all ten sit in a similar brightness band. Merging, Unbarred Tight Spiral and Barred Spiral are slightly brighter, while In-between Smooth, Round Smooth and Disturbed are slightly darker, but no class stands out.

Color does not separate the classes. Shape carries the signal, and shape is exactly what rotation affects. The research question is therefore relevant to the whole task, not just part of it.

**![][image5]**

### **3.8 Rotational self-similarity**

We measured how similar each galaxy looks to its own 90-degree-rotated version using SSIM (structural similarity). Images were centre-cropped first so that background stars did not affect the score.

**What we expected:** Round Smooth galaxies are close to circularly symmetric, so they should score highest. Spirals have directional arm structure, so they should score lowest.

**What we found:** The opposite. The median SSIM scores were:

| Class | Median SSIM | Class | Median SSIM |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Barred Spiral | 0.324 | Disturbed | 0.264 |
| Round Smooth | 0.295 | In-between Smooth | 0.255 |
| Unbarred Tight Spiral | 0.291 | Unbarred Loose Spiral | 0.248 |
|  |  | Merging | 0.242 |
|  |  | Cigar-shaped Smooth | 0.209 |

Barred Spiral scored highest and Round Smooth was only third.

SSIM is a fairly coarse measure. It responds mainly to the overall brightness envelope of an image rather than to fine detail such as exact arm placement. Spiral galaxies keep a roughly circular light profile when rotated (a bright centre fading outward), so that envelope survives rotation well. Round Smooth galaxies are so low-contrast that there is little structure for the metric to compare in the first place, which is consistent with them dominating the low-variance images in section 3.4.

This gave us a second prediction to test later: that spirals would hold up under rotation while smooth classes would not.

**![][image6]**

### **3.9 EDA summary**

| Finding | Consequence for the project |
| :---- | :---- |
| No corrupted or blank images | The data can be used as-is |
| Classes are imbalanced, about 8 to 1 | Report per-class metrics and a confusion matrix |
| Colour does not separate classes | Shape carries the signal, so rotation is relevant to the whole task |
| Some classes lie on a continuum | Expect confusion between spiral sub-types |
| Two independent predictions made | Edge-on and Merging at risk from clipping; smooth classes at risk per SSIM |

## **4\. Building the baseline model**

### **4.1 Data preparation**

**Splitting:** We split the data three ways using stratified sampling, which preserves the class proportions in each part, with a fixed random seed so the split is reproducible.

| Split | Size | Purpose |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Train | 12,415 | What the model learns from |
| Validation | 2,660 | Used for every model-selection decision |
| Test | 2,661 | Held out and untouched until the final evaluation |

The three-way split matters. If we used the test set to choose the epoch or the architecture, our final number would be optimistic. Keeping it untouched means the number we report is honest.

**Preprocessing:** Each image is resized to 224x224, which is the input size the pretrained models expect, converted to a tensor with pixel values scaled to 0 to 1, and normalised using the standard ImageNet channel means and standard deviations. That last step matters because the pretrained weights were trained on data normalised the same way.

We deliberately did not apply any augmentation in the baseline. Augmentation is the variable we test in sub-question 2, so including it in the baseline would have destroyed the comparison.

**Loading:** A custom Dataset class applies the preprocessing to one image at a time on demand, rather than transforming all 17,736 images up front, which keeps memory use low. DataLoaders serve batches of 64 images, shuffled for training and unshuffled for validation and test.

### **4.2 Transfer learning**

Training a deep network from scratch on 17,000+ images would be slow and would not work well. So we used transfer learning: start from a network already trained on ImageNet, which has learned to detect generic visual features such as edges, curves and textures, and adapt it to galaxies.

The adaptation has three parts:

Freeze the whole pretrained network so its learned features are not disturbed.

Unfreeze the final block, so the most task-specific layers can adapt to galaxy images.

Replace the final layer, which outputs 1,000 ImageNet categories, with a fresh layer that outputs our 10 classes \- This new layer is trainable by default.

The early layers stay frozen because edge and curve detectors transfer to any image task without modification. Only the later, more specialised layers need to change.

### **4.3 First baseline with ResNet-18**

We started with ResNet-18 to confirm the pipeline works end to end before comparing architectures. ResNet-18 is a sensible default: its residual (skip) connections allow deep networks to train without vanishing gradients, it includes batch normalisation, and it is small and fast.

With the final block and the new head unfrozen, the model had 8,398,858 trainable parameters. The reason is that deeper layers in a CNN are much wider (more channels), so they hold most of the weights. Freezing three of the four blocks does not freeze most of the parameters.

**Results on a development subset (2,800 training images):**

| Epoch | Train loss | Validation accuracy |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 1 | 1.784 | 0.480 |
| 2 | 0.967 | 0.527 |
| 3 | 0.524 | 0.538 |
| 4 | 0.221 | 0.552 |
| 5 | 0.088 | 0.563 |

The training loss collapses towards zero while validation accuracy stays flat around 56 percent. That gap is the signature of overfitting: the model is memorising the training images rather than learning patterns that generalise.

### **4.4 Scaling up to the full dataset**

We repeated the identical setup on the full dataset, changing only the amount of data. We built a fresh model rather than continuing to train the overfitted one, so the two runs stay independent and comparable.

Validation accuracy rose from about 56% to about 67-68%, an improvement of roughly 11 points. Running it twice gave 0.674 and 0.679, so the result is stable and the run-to-run noise is around 1 point. That noise figure is useful later: it tells us how large a difference has to be before it means anything.

The model still overfits \- Validation accuracy peaked at epoch 2 and did not improve after that, while training loss kept falling to about 0.02. Everything after epoch 2 added memorisation, not learning.

**What we changed as a result.** From this point on we save the checkpoint with the best validation accuracy rather than using whatever the final epoch produces, so each model is judged at its own best point.

## **5\. Choosing a backbone**

### **5.1 The four candidates**

ResNet-18 is only one option, and the effect of architecture is one of our sub-questions, so we compared four pretrained networks representing three different design ideas.

| Backbone | Design idea |
| :---- | :---- |
| ResNet-18 | Residual (skip) connections |
| VGG-16 | A plain deep stack of small 3x3 filters, no skip connections |
| EfficientNet-B0 | Depthwise-separable convolutions with compound scaling |
| MobileNetV2 | Lightweight depthwise-separable design |

Everything was held constant except the architecture: same data split, same preprocessing, same optimizer, same learning rate, same epoch budget, and best-validation checkpointing for all.

### **5.2 A fairness problem we found and fixed**

Our first comparison had a flaw that we caught before drawing conclusions from it.

**The problem.** We applied one rule to every model: “unfreeze the last block”. But a block means something different in each architecture- In ResNet and VGG the final block contains several million parameters. In the depthwise-separable models it contains far fewer. The result was that ResNet and VGG received roughly 7 to 8 million trainable parameters while EfficientNet and MobileNet received only about 1 million.

Since accuracy depends heavily on how much of the network can adapt, we were not comparing architectures at all. We were comparing how much capacity we happened to give each one. The scatter plot of accuracy against parameter count was close to a straight line, which is what made us suspicious.

**The fix:** We resized the unfrozen portion of each model so that all four had comparable trainable capacity, and we extended the budget from 4 to 10 epochs.

**The effect:** MobileNetV2 improved by 16 percentage points and EfficientNet-B0 by 19\. Their earlier scores were not telling us anything about those architectures, only about our freezing rule.

**A second problem, also fixed:** In the first attempt every model peaked at the final epoch, which means none of them had finished improving. A comparison between under-trained models is not meaningful. After extending to 10 epochs, all four converged within the budget, and we added an automatic warning that fires if any model peaks at the last epoch.

**![][image7]**

### **5.3 Results**

| Backbone | Best validation accuracy | Best epoch | Trainable parameters | Training time |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| VGG-16 | 0.758 | 6 | 7,120,394 | 16.4 min |
| MobileNetV2 | 0.685 | 3 | 1,812,426 | 6.6 min |
| EfficientNet-B0 | 0.682 | 8 | 3,711,698 | 8.0 min |
| ResNet-18 | 0.674 | 2 | 8,398,858 | 6.4 min |

Three things stand out:

**VGG-16 wins clearly-** Its lead of 7 to 8 points is far beyond the roughly 1 point of run-to-run noise we measured earlier, so the result is real.

**The models converge at very different speeds-** ResNet peaked at epoch 2 while EfficientNet needed 8\. This is exactly why the longer budget mattered: a short budget would have penalised the slower models unfairly.

**Capacity does not explain accuracy-** ResNet-18 has the most trainable parameters and the lowest score while mobileNetV2 has the fewest and still beats it. Once capacity was equalised, the ranking reflected architecture rather than size.

**One caveat-** The lower three models fall within about 1 point of each other, which is inside our noise range. We therefore do not rank them against one another. The reliable conclusion is that VGG-16 leads and the other three are comparable.

### **5.4 Decision**

We adopted VGG-16 as the baseline for the rest of the project. The trade-off is training time: it takes about 2.5 times longer than ResNet-18.

We kept all four trained models, because sub-question 3 asks about the effect of architecture on robustness, and reusing these checkpoints means that experiment costs no extra training. Since accuracy here is not explained by capacity, the robustness ranking may well differ from the accuracy ranking.

## **6\. Baseline evaluation**

### **6.1 Test set results**

We loaded the best VGG-16 checkpoint and evaluated it once on the held-out test set of 2,661 images that had not influenced any decision.

| Metric | Value |
| :---- | :---- |
| Test accuracy | 73.4% |
| Validation accuracy | 75.8% |
| Difference | 2.4 points |

The test score being slightly lower than validation is expected and healthy. We used the validation set to pick the epoch and the architecture, so it is mildly optimistic. The test set influenced nothing, so it is the honest number. A small gap tells us we did not overfit our model-selection choices.

### **6.2 Per-class performance**

| Class | Recall |
| :---- | :---- |
| Edge-on without Bulge | 0.892 |
| Edge-on with Bulge | 0.879 |
| Round Smooth | 0.877 |
| Merging | 0.820 |
| Cigar-shaped Smooth | 0.800 |
| Barred Spiral | 0.798 |
| In-between Smooth | 0.720 |
| Unbarred Loose Spiral | 0.581 |
| Unbarred Tight Spiral | 0.575 |
| Disturbed | 0.309 |

Recall answers “of all the real galaxies of this type, how many did the model find”. Precision answers “when the model predicts this type, how often is it right”. The two can diverge. In-between Smooth has high precision (0.880) but lower recall (0.720), meaning the model is cautious with that class: it is rarely wrong when it predicts it, but it misses many real cases. Cigar-shaped Smooth shows the opposite pattern (precision 0.506, recall 0.800), meaning it over-predicts that class.

Macro average recall (0.725) and weighted average recall (0.734) are close, which indicates that performance is not dominated by the class imbalance.

### **6.3 Error analysis**

The mistakes are not random. They cluster exactly where the class definitions genuinely blur.

**Disturbed to Unbarred Loose Spiral (47 images, 29% of the class).** Disturbed is a broad label for irregular structure, and such galaxies really do look like untidy spirals.

**The three spiral types confuse with each other-** Unbarred Tight Spiral loses 58 images (21%) to Loose Spiral and 30 (11%) to Barred Spiral. Unbarred Loose Spiral loses 49 (12%) to Barred Spiral and 40 (10%) to Tight Spiral. In total, 75% of all Tight Spiral errors are predictions of some other spiral class. These are not separate categories but points along a continuum describing how tightly the arms wind and whether a bar is present, so there is no sharp visual boundary. Even human labellers disagree in the same places.

**In-between Smooth to Round Smooth (33 images, 11%)-** The same continuum problem in the smooth family. “In-between” is defined by degree of roundness, not by a distinct feature.

**Cigar-shaped Smooth to Edge-on with Bulge (6 images, 12%of this small class)-**Both are elongated shapes, and a smooth cigar looks much like a disk seen edge-on.

**Interpretation:** The model does well on classes defined by a distinctive overall shape and poorly on classes that sit on a continuum or depend on subjective judgement. This is a reasonable failure mode rather than a broken model.

**![][image8]**

## **7\. Sub-question 1: measuring robustness**

### **7.1 Method**

We took the trained baseline and evaluated it repeatedly on the same test set, applying a controlled transformation each time: rotations from 0 to 345 degrees in 15 degree steps, plus horizontal and vertical flips.

**A control built into the design:** Rotating a square image leaves empty corners. The model might react to those corners rather than to the orientation, which would invalidate the whole experiment. To prevent this we rotate the full image first and then centre-crop to 180x180, which is the largest centred square that contains no empty region at any rotation angle. This same crop is applied at every angle including 0 degrees, so rotation is the only variable that changes across the sweep.

One consequence is that the 0 degree accuracy in this section is lower than the 73.4% reported in section 6, because the cropped pipeline differs from the one used there. The correct reference point for this experiment is its own 0 degree value, not the earlier number.

**![][image9]**

### **7.2 Rotation results**

Accuracy follows a clear pattern with a period of 90 degrees. It peaks at exactly 0, 90, 180 and 270 degrees and dips at every angle in between.

**![][image10]**

### **7.3 Flip results**

Horizontal and vertical flips did not reduce accuracy at all. Both produced results equal to or slightly better than the unflipped baseline.

This is worth noting because ImageNet pretraining conventionally includes random horizontal flips as augmentation, so the pretrained features already encode some flip invariance. Rotation augmentation is not standard, so no equivalent rotation invariance was learned during pretraining.

**![][image11]**

### **7.4 Per-class degradation**

We compared per-class recall at 0 degrees against an intermediate angle to see which classes break down.

The classes that degraded most were the smooth ones. The edge-on classes, which we had predicted would be the most vulnerable, were essentially unchanged.

The most informative case is Round Smooth. It is close to rotationally symmetric, so rotating it should change almost nothing. Yet it lost about 11 points. Orientation cannot explain that.

### **7.5 The problem with the obvious interpretation**

At first glance the sawtooth curve looks like proof that the model is not rotation invariant. But the pattern does not fit that explanation.

A 90 degree rotation completely reorients the galaxy, and it costs nothing. If the model were sensitive to orientation, 90 degrees should hurt as much as 45 degrees, and it does not. So the damage is not caused by how much the galaxy is turned.

What actually separates the harmful angles from the harmless ones is whether the rotation is an exact pixel remapping. Rotations using bilinear interpolations by multiples of 90 degrees, and flips, simply move pixels to new positions with no loss. Intermediate angles require the computer to invent pixel values by interpolating between neighbours, which slightly blurs the image.

This gives two competing explanations, orientation sensitivity and interpolation blur, and both predict exactly the same sawtooth. The experiment as designed cannot tell them apart.

### **7.6 The control experiment \- Checking the cause of the accuracy drop**

**Design:** Rotate each image by \+θ, then by \-θ. The galaxy ends up in its original orientation, but it has passed through two interpolation steps instead of one.

If orientation is what matters, accuracy should be normal, because the image is upright. If interpolation is what matters, accuracy should still drop, because the image has been interpolated twice.

**Results:**

| Condition | Accuracy | Drop vs 0 degrees | Net reorientation |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 0 degree reference | 0.6798 | \- | none |
| ±15 degrees | 0.6389 | 4.1 points | none |
| ±30 degrees | 0.6370 | 4.3 points | none |
| ±45 degrees | 0.6343 | 4.6 points | none |
| ±60 degrees | 0.6362 | 4.4 points | none |

Accuracy falls by 4.1 to 4.6 points even though the images were never reoriented.

**The comparison that settles it:** The control is worse than the real rotation at every angle we tested: 0.6389 against 0.6652 at 15 degrees, 0.6370 against 0.6524 at 30 degrees, 0.6343 against 0.6479 at 45 degrees, and 0.6362 against 0.6486 at 60 degrees. The doubly-rotated image is perfectly upright and still does worse than the singly-rotated image that is not.

This is a dose-response relationship. More interpolation causes more damage. The degradation tracks the number of interpolation steps, not the amount of reorientation.

The gap narrows as the angle grows, from 2.6 points at 15 degrees down to 1.2 at 60\. That is consistent with a single interpolation pass already causing most of the achievable damage at larger angles.

### **7.7 Conclusion for sub-question 1**

The baseline is robust to orientation. Flips cost nothing, and rotations by exact multiples of 90 degrees leave accuracy unchanged even though they completely reorient the galaxy.

The drop at intermediate angles is caused by image quality, not orientation. Those rotations require interpolation, which slightly blurs the image, and the control experiment demonstrates this directly by reproducing the drop with no net reorientation at all.

The per-class pattern supports the same conclusion. The classes that suffer most are the smooth ones, which are distinguished by subtle brightness gradients that blurring degrades. The structurally distinctive edge-on and spiral classes hold up well.

## **8\. Sub-question 2: data augmentation**

### **8.1 Method**

Data augmentation means applying random transformations to training images so the model never sees exactly the same picture twice. Here, each galaxy is randomly rotated to a new angle and randomly flipped every time it is shown during training. The label does not change.

Augmentation is applied to training data only. Validation and test data stay unmodified, so our measurements remain honest.

**An extra control:** The original baseline was trained on full images, but the rotation sweep evaluates centre-cropped images, and that mismatch alone is worth about 7 points. If we compared an augmented model trained with cropping against the original uncropped baseline, part of any improvement would come from the cropping rather than from augmentation.

To avoid this we retrained both models under the same crop pipeline:

vgg16\_crop: cropping, no augmentation

vgg16\_aug: cropping plus random rotations and flips

Everything else was identical, so augmentation is the only difference between them.

### **8.2 Training behaviour**

The two models behaved very differently during training:

|  | Without augmentation | With augmentation |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Best validation accuracy | 0.776 at epoch 7 | 0.788 at epoch 10 |
| Final training loss | 0.109 | 0.556 |
| Pattern | Overfits after epoch 7 | Still improving at epoch 10 |

Without augmentation the model overfits in the familiar way: training loss falls towards zero while validation accuracy slips from 0.776 down to 0.752.

With augmentation the training loss stays high at 0.556, because the task is genuinely harder when every image appears in a new orientation, and validation accuracy keeps climbing. It never overfits.

So augmentation is doing two jobs at once here: improving robustness, and acting as regularisation.

### **8.3 Results**

| Metric | Baseline (cropped) | Augmented | Change |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Accuracy at 0 degrees | 0.7550 | 0.7632 | \+0.8 points |
| Mean across all angles | 0.7493 | 0.7737 | \+2.4 points |
| Worst angle | 0.7373 | 0.7561 | \+1.9 points |
| Drop from 0 to worst | 0.0177 | 0.0071 | smaller |

The augmented model scored higher at all 24 angles tested. There was no trade-off anywhere.

**Where the gains are concentrated:** This is the part that connects back to sub-question 1\. At the exact rotations (0, 90, 180, 270 degrees), which were already fine, the improvement is small, \+0.7 to \+1.0 points. At the intermediate angles, where interpolation had been hurting the model, the improvement is much larger, reaching \+4.0 points at 225 degrees.

That is exactly what the interpolation explanation predicts. Training on randomly rotated images means training on interpolated, slightly blurred images, so the model learns to handle the specific degradation that was hurting it.

**What did not change:** The 90 degree sawtooth is still present in the augmented curve. Augmentation did not remove the interpolation effect. It raised the whole curve and made the model more tolerant of it.

**![][image12]**

### **8.4 Convergence check**

The augmented model was still improving at epoch 10, which meant our numbers might have been an underestimate. We retrained it for 15 epochs to check.

It peaked at epoch 10 with a validation accuracy of 0.801 and then plateaued. On the rotation sweep the two versions were effectively identical, with mean accuracies of 0.7737 for the 10 epoch model and 0.7713 for the 15 epoch model, a difference of 0.24 points which is well inside our noise range.

Ten epochs was enough- We adopted the 10 epoch model as our augmented result.

**![][image13]**

### **8.5 Conclusion for sub-question 2**

Rotation and flip augmentation improves robustness by 2.4 points on average, with the gains concentrated at the angles that interpolation had degraded. It also improves upright accuracy slightly and prevents the overfitting seen in the baseline.

The mechanism is consistent with sub-question 1\. Augmentation is not teaching the model to handle orientation, because it already could. It is teaching the model to tolerate interpolation artefacts.

## **9\. Sub-question 3: architecture**

### **9.1 Method**

We had already trained and saved all four backbones during backbone selection, so this experiment required no additional training. We applied the identical rotation sweep to each model.

We measured two different things:

**Accuracy**, meaning how high the curve sits.

**Robustness**, meaning how flat the curve is, measured by the range between best and worst angle and by the standard deviation across angles. A flatter curve means a more rotation-robust model.

The key question was whether the most accurate architecture is also the most robust. They do not have to be the same model, and if they differ it would show that architecture affects robustness independently of accuracy.

### **9.2 Results**

| Backbone | Mean accuracy | Range (max \- min) | Std | Relative drop |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| VGG-16 | 0.649 | 0.051 | 0.0135 | 7.9% |
| ResNet-18 | 0.555 | 0.076 | 0.0202 | 13.8% |
| MobileNetV2 | 0.549 | 0.061 | 0.0186 | 11.2% |
| EfficientNet-B0 | 0.467 | 0.116 | 0.0345 | 24.8% |

**VGG-16 is best on both measures-** It is the most accurate and it has the flattest curve, which confirms that our baseline choice was well founded.

**All four architectures show the same sawtooth**, with the same period and the same phase. This is the strongest single piece of evidence for the interpolation explanation. That pattern belongs to the rotation operation, not to any particular architecture.

**Accuracy and robustness track together, but not perfectly.** The two rankings agree at the extremes, with VGG-16 best on both and EfficientNet-B0 worst on both, but they swap in the middle. MobileNetV2 is more robust than ResNet-18 despite being slightly less accurate. So architecture influences robustness partly independently of accuracy.

**EfficientNet-B0 is an outlier**, noticeably lower and more jagged than the others. Since EfficientNet is generally considered a strong architecture, this most likely reflects our fine-tuning setup rather than a real weakness. Depthwise-separable networks often need more of the network unfrozen, or a different learning rate, to perform well.

![][image14]

### **9.3 Conclusion for sub-question 3**

Architecture affects both accuracy and rotational robustness. More accurate architectures tend to be more robust, VGG-16 leads on both measures, and the shared sawtooth across all four models confirms that the degradation mechanism is universal.

## **10\. Conclusions**

### **10.1 Summary of findings**

**Sub-question 1-** The baseline is robust to orientation. Flips and 90 degree rotations cost nothing. Accuracy drops only at intermediate angles, and a control experiment showed that this drop is caused by interpolation blur rather than by orientation sensitivity. Rotating an image by \+θ and then \-θ, which leaves it upright but interpolated twice, reproduced the drop in full and in fact produced worse results than the real rotation at every angle tested.

**Sub-question 2-** Rotation and flip augmentation improves robustness by 2.4 points on average, with gains concentrated at the previously degraded angles. It also improves upright accuracy and prevents overfitting. Ten epochs was sufficient for convergence.

**Sub-question 3-** Architecture affects both accuracy and robustness. VGG-16 is best on both. All four architectures show the same 90 degree sawtooth, which independently confirms that the effect belongs to the rotation operation itself.

### **10.2 Main takeaway**

The central result is the opposite of what we expected when we started. A standard transfer-learned CNN is already largely rotation invariant for this task. What looks at first like a robustness failure is mostly an artefact of the image degradation introduced when an image is rotated.

We would not have found this without the control experiment. The first sweep produced a convincing sawtooth curve, and the obvious reading of that curve was wrong. Being able to separate the two explanations is the main contribution of this project.

### **10.3 Limitations**

* All backbones were pretrained on ImageNet, which consists of natural photographs. Astronomical images are quite different, being mostly dark sky with a small bright object. Domain-specific pretraining might change the results.  
* Most results come from single training runs. We measured about 1 point of run-to-run variation, so differences smaller than that should not be read as meaningful.  
* The classes are imbalanced, and the hardest classes lie on a genuine morphological continuum where even human labels disagree.  
* We fine-tuned only the final block of each network. A different fine-tuning strategy could change the architecture comparison, and this particularly affects EfficientNet-B0.  
* The 180x180 centre crop used in the robustness sweep removes some outer image area, which lowers absolute accuracy relative to the full-image pipeline. This is consistent across all angles, so it does not affect the comparisons, but it does mean the sweep numbers are not directly comparable to the section 6 test accuracy.

### **10.4 Future work**

* Repeat the sweep with higher-quality interpolation, or rotate at full resolution before downsampling, to further isolate the interpolation effect. If the dips shrink, that confirms the mechanism and also gives a practical recommendation for evaluating rotated astronomical images.  
* Test rotation-equivariant architectures, which build rotational symmetry into the network by construction rather than learning it from data. This would be a stronger alternative to augmentation and would need less data to achieve the same invariance.  
* Try test-time augmentation, averaging predictions over several rotations at inference. This costs no additional training and might recover some of the lost accuracy.  
* Run each configuration with multiple random seeds and report mean and standard deviation, so that small differences can be interpreted with confidence.
